Empirical Research Plan  
“Scars of War: The Long-Run Economic Impact of WWII Bombing on Japanese Cities”

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) in a city-by-year panel, augmented with an event-study (dynamic DID) to trace short-, medium-, and long-run effects.

Why DID?  
• The intensity of Allied bombing varied sharply across cities in 1944-45, while macroeconomic, political, and institutional environments were common to all Japanese cities.  
• City-specific fixed effects absorb time-invariant heterogeneity (geography, historical importance).  
• Year fixed effects capture nationwide shocks (post-war reconstruction policy, macro cycles).  
• The timing of the “treatment” is common (WWII bombings in 1945), but the dose differs, making a staggered/binary DID or dose–response DID appropriate.  
• Event-study coefficients provide a built-in pre-trend test and allow us to map recovery dynamics.

Secondary analyses:  
• Dose-response regressions (continuous bombing intensity).  
• IV robustness: instrument bombing intensity with distance to the closest military target * interacted with prevailing wind patterns. (Only as a robustness extension; core results will not rely on the IV).

------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Main binary specification: Treated = 1 if a city’s share of buildings destroyed ≥ median destruction rate (≈ 25%) or if incendiary tonnage per km² ≥ median.  
Continuous specification: BombIntensity = % of built-up area destroyed or log(tons/km² dropped).

Control group  
Cities below the median destruction rate (or bottom tercile in robustness checks). These cities were still subject to wartime dislocation but escaped major physical destruction.

Timing  
Treatment date = 1945. All pre-1945 observations are “pre”; 1945 onward are “post”. For dynamics, we create event-time dummies k = …-5,…,0,1,…,T relative to 1945.

------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel pre-trends: In the absence of bombing, treated and control cities would have followed similar trajectories in population and economic activity.  
Plausibility: Pre-war series (1920-1940) show very similar growth paths across size categories; military targeting was guided by production capacity, but we control flexibly for pre-war industrial employment and interactions with year FE.

A2. Exogeneity of bombing intensity conditional on observables: After controlling for pre-war city size and industry, residual variation in destruction is quasi-random (affected by weather, availability of aircraft, pilot error).  
Plausibility: Historical literature documents substantial randomness; we will also test with an IV (distance × wind).

A3. No spillovers violating SUTVA: Outcomes in lightly bombed cities are not directly affected by destruction elsewhere (e.g., displaced firms relocating).  
Plausibility: Some spillovers likely exist; we mitigate by excluding nearest-neighbor controls and by checking spatial clustering.

A4. Stable composition of cities: Administrative boundaries and city definitions remain comparable over time.  
Plausibility: Japanese municipal mergers occurred mainly in the 1950s; we harmonize boundaries to 1935 borders.

------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Targeting correlated with pre-war industrial strength  
• Mitigation: Control for 1930 employment by sector, interact with year FE, and run matched-sample estimators (propensity score matching + DID).  
• IV robustness using distance × wind pattern.

T2. Post-war migration/relocation (spillovers)  
• Mitigation: Estimate population effects using birthplace-cohort censuses (people born in city i) to separate in-migration from birth effects.  
• Spatial HAC or Conley standard errors and exclusion of nearest neighbors.

T3. Mean-reversion / regression to the mean  
• Mitigation: Include city-specific linear time trends and check results with first-difference specification over 10-year intervals.

------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------------------------------------
install.packages(c("fixest","tidyverse","data.table","sandwich","lmtest"))
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional fixed effects
library(tidyverse)
library(data.table)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load & prepare data
# -------------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("japan_city_bombing_panel.csv")   # city-year panel 1920-1980

# Consistent city identifier
dt <- dt %>%
  mutate(city_id = as.integer(city_id),
         year    = as.integer(year))

# Treatment indicators
median_destr <- median(dt$destruction_rate[dt$year == 1945], na.rm = TRUE)
dt <- dt %>%
  mutate(treated         = ifelse(destruction_rate >= median_destr & year >= 1945, 1, 0),
         post            = ifelse(year >= 1945, 1, 0),
         bomb_intensity  = destruction_rate,                     # continuous
         event_time      = year - 1945)

# Event-study dummies k = -10 to +35
max_k <- 35; min_k <- -10
for(k in min_k:max_k){
  dt[[paste0("event_",k)]] <- as.numeric(dt$event_time == k)
}

# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Main DID (binary treatment)
# -------------------------------------------------------------
did_bin <- feols(log(population) ~ treated + post + i(year) | city_id + year, data = dt,
                 cluster = ~city_id)
summary(did_bin)

# DID with continuous dosage
did_cont <- feols(log(population) ~ bomb_intensity*post | city_id + year,
                  data = dt, cluster = ~city_id)
summary(did_cont)

# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Event-study (Sun & Abraham style)
# -------------------------------------------------------------
# collapse dynamic dummies into relative years, exclude k = -1
event_vars <- paste0("event_", setdiff(min_k:max_k, -1))
formula_event <- as.formula(paste("log(population) ~", 
                                   paste(event_vars, collapse = " + "),
                                   "| city_id + year"))
event_model <- feols(formula_event, data = dt, cluster = ~city_id)
iplot(event_model, ref.line = -1, xlab = "Years since 1945", ylab = "Log Pop effect")

# -------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: matched sample (PSM + DID)
# -------------------------------------------------------------
library(MatchIt)
prewar <- dt %>% filter(year == 1940) %>% 
            select(city_id, destruction_rate, pre_pop = population, pre_ind_employ)
m.out <- matchit(destruction_rate >= median_destr ~ log(pre_pop) + pre_ind_employ,
                 data = prewar, distance = "logit", ratio = 1)
matched_ids <- match.data(m.out)$city_id
dt_match <- dt %>% filter(city_id %in% matched_ids)

did_match <- feols(log(population) ~ treated + post | city_id + year,
                   data = dt_match, cluster = ~city_id)
summary(did_match)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------------
Hypothesis: Heavier WWII bombing caused a sharp immediate drop in population and economic activity (factories destroyed, housing loss), but effects partially dissipated as Japan’s rapid post-war reconstruction and government aid rebuilt capacity.

Magnitude (rough priors, log points):  
• Population: –0.30 to –0.40 log points (≈ 25–33 %) in 1950, narrowing to –0.05 to –0.10 by 1980.  
• Economic output (taxable sales / manufacturing value added): –0.40 to –0.50 initially; converging to 0 or a small negative gap (< –0.10) by 1980.

------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (for DID)

C1: Common pre-treatment trends verified via event-study = 1  
C2: No significant differential anticipation (pre-1945) = 1  
C3: No spillovers / SUTVA ≈ 0 (concern remains)  
C4: Accurate treatment timing & no contamination = 1  
C5: Stable composition / consistent measurement = 1  

Total = 4 / 5.
